1. Allocation Functions elt refers to the process of dividing resources between public goods and private goods, essentially deciding which social services and infrastructure projects to fund.
2. Redistribution Functions elt aims to reduce income inequality by using progressive taxation (higher tax rates for higher earners) and providing social welfare programs like unemployment benefits.

3. Stabilisation Functions elt is aimed at maintaining economic stability by adjusting government spending and taxation to counter recession (by increasing spending) or inflation (by decreasing spending).
An asset is a resource with economic value that an individual, a company, or a country owns or controls with the expectation that it will provide a future benefit. E.g.
A liability represents the obligation or responsibility to fulfill a debt or duty to another party. E.g. Payment of loan.
Budget is divided into two heads: Revenue and Capital.

Revenue refers to the funds that a government collects to finance its activities and public services. This primarily comes from taxes, as well as other sources like fees, fines, and duties. elt is of two types: Revenue Receipts and Revenue Expenditure Revenue Receipts These are earnings that do not create liabilities or reduce assets. eRevenue Receipts do not lead to claim on government and are of non-redeemable in nature.
1. Tax Revenue: The income that is collected by governments through taxation. Eg. Wealth tax.
2. Non-Tax Revenue: It is the recurring income that is earned from sources other than taxes by the government.
E.g. Interest on loans, PSU earnings, railway tickets.
It is the amount of money spent that does not lead to increase in assets nor decrease in liabilities.
1. Plan Revenue Expenditure: It is a government expenditure that is part of the plan budget and does not create assets or liabilities. E.g. Government grants/financial assistance.

2. Non-Plan Revenue Expenditure: It is the money a government spends on its day-to-day operations, excluding capital expenditures. Eg. Salary/pension, interest payment (largest component of non-plan expenditure), maintenance of infrastructure.
Capital elt is the physical or financial resources that is used to produce value in an economy. elt is of two types: Capital Receipts and Capital Expenditures.

1. Capital Receipt: They are those receipts which either create liabilities or reduce the asset value of the government. It creates new liabilities and reduces an existing asset. E.g. Loan, disinvestment.

2. Capital Expenditure: It refers to the funds that organizations or governments allocate to acquire, upgrade, or maintain long-term assets such as property, infrastructure, or equipment. It creates new assets for government and reduces liabilities. E.g. Loan repayment, loan granted, developmental expenditure, infrastructure creation (roads, schools, hospitals).
Central Government will target reaching a debt-to-GDP ratio of 50+1 % by 2030.

The debt-to-GDP ratio is estimated to be 55.6 % of GDP in BE 2026-27, compared to 56.1 % of GDP in RE 2025-26. eIn RE 2025-26, the fiscal deficit has been estimated at par with BE of 2025-26 at 4.4 % of GDP. In line with the new fiscal prudence path of debt consolidation, the fiscal deficit in BE 2026-27 is estimated to be 4.3 % of GDP.

Kelkar committee (2002-03): recommended the simplification of direct taxes in post-liberalisation India Kelkar Committee (2015): recommended improving the PPP model to enhance efficiency and transparency in infrastructure projects The Raja Chelliah Committee (1991) was set up to reform India's tax system. It recommended reducing personal income tax and corporate tax rates, widening the tax base by removing unnecessary exemptions, simplifying the tax structure, expanding the MODVAT scheme to avoid cascading of taxes, and gradually reducing high customs duties to make the tax system more efficient and growth- oriented.
Taxation System in India Direct Tax eThese taxes are directly payable to the government.
It cannot be passed onto someone else.
Direct taxes are progressive in nature.
Here, the marginal tax rate is greater than the average tax rate.
E.g. Income tax, wealth tax, gift tax, capital gain tax, corporate tax.
These are indirectly payable to the government.
It can be passed onto someone else.
Indirect taxes are regressive/proportional in nature.
E.g. GST, Excise Duty (petrol, diesel, aviation turbine fuel), Custom Duty.
Tax which carry their significance only on paper and have no significance in terms of revenue yield are called paper taxes.
E.g. Wealth tax, gift tax, estate duty (not levied now)
The Laffer curve is a graph that shows the relationship between the tax rates and government revenue.
The curve suggests that increasing taxes beyond a certain point can actually decrease the revenue.
This is because higher taxes can discourage investment and consumption, and workers may work less if they believe their extra efforts result in lower income.

WMaA,1997 (Ways and Means Advances) Agreement As per the agreement, the Central Government would ss temporary mismatches between receipts and expenditure through Ways and Means Advances (WMA) provided by the RBI.
Purpose: To manage temporary shortages in government cash flow, not a permanent source of finance.
Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003 (FRBM)
The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM)

Act was enacted to ensure fiscal discipline and responsible financial management by the Government of India. eThe FRBM Act was passed in 2003 to reduce fiscal deficit and improve transparency in government finances. It aimed to limit fiscal deficit to around 3% of GDP and promote prudent management of public debt.
It was formed on May 2016 and headed by NK Singh. He gave few recommendation as below eDebt-GDP Target: Total public debt should be 60% of GDP (40% for Centre + 20% for States).
Fiscal Deficit Target: Reduce fiscal deficit to 2.5% of GDP in the medium term by 2023
Escape Clause: Government can deviate from fiscal deficit target by 0.5% of GDP in exceptional situations like war, national security issues, natural disasters, or economic slowdown by 2023

Fiscal Council: Recommended setting up an independent Fiscal Council to monitor fiscal discipline 1. Medium Term Fiscal Policy Statement: This statement outlines a 3-year rolling target for key fiscal indicators, such as revenue and fiscal deficits etc.
2. Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement: This outlines the government's financial goals and the methods it plans to use to achieve them.
3. Macroeconomic Framework Statement: This provides an overview of the country's economic situation, · Crowding In:
Crowding in occurs when government spending (especially on infrastructure and public investment) encourages and stimulates private sector investment, leading to higher overall economic activity.
Crowding Out:

Crowding out occurs when increased government borrowing or expenditure raises interest rates and reduces private sector investment, as the government competes with the private sector for available funds.
A Budget can be classified into three types:
1. Balanced Budget: It is a condition where the total revenues are equivalent to the total expenditure (Receipt = Expenditure).
2. Surplus Budget: It is a condition when _ total income or receipts exceeds its total expenditures (Receipt > Expenditure).
3. Deficit Budget: It is a condition when expenses exceed the revenue (Expenditure > Receipt).
Deficit Financing (By J.M Keynes)
Deficit financing refers to a situation where government expenditure exceeds its revenue and the gap is financed by creating new money or by borrowing funds.
Methods of Deficit Financing: Debt Financing:
It refers to raising funds through borrowing, where the government or a firm takes loans from banks, financial institutions, or issues bonds and the amount must be repaid with interest.
Equity Financing:
It refers to raising funds by issuing shares, where investors become owners (shareholders) of the company and share in profits through dividends, without any obligation to repay the capital.
A deficit is when the expenses exceed revenue.

1. Budgetary Deficit: It occurs when government's total expenditures exceed its total revenues from taxes and other sources. This indicates that the government is spending more than it is earning, leading to borrowing.
2. Revenue Deficit: It occurs when a government's revenue expenditure exceeds its revenue receipts.
3. Effective Revenue Deficit: It is the difference between revenue deficit and grants used to create capital assets.

Effective Revenue Deficit = Revenue Deficit - Grant given for the developmental purpose 4. Fiscal Deficit: It represents the total borrowing requirement of government. It occurs when total government expenditure exceeds the sum of total receipts (excluding borrowings).
Fiscal Deficit = Total Exp - [Total receipt-Debt creating Capital Receipt)
Total expenditure - (RR+Non debt Capital Receipt)
5. Primary Deficit: It is defined as the difference between the fiscal deficit and the previous year interest payments of the government.

Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit - Interest Payment _ Externalities: An externality is an indirect cost or benefit to an uninvolved third party that arises as an effect of _ another party's activity. It can be Positive or Negative.

16th Finance Commission The Finance Commission is a constitutional body under Article 280 of the Constitution of India, constituted by the President every 5 years to recommend the distribution of tax revenues between the Centre and the States.
The 16th Finance Commission was constituted on 31 December 2023 under Article 280(1) of the Constitution.
The Chairman is Arvind Panagariya and the commission consists of 1 Chairman and 4 Members.
Its functions include recommending:
Vertical Devolution — It refers to the share of the total divisible pool of central taxes given to all states collectively.

The Government has accepted the recommendation of the Finance Commission to retain the vertical share of devolution at 41%. eHorizontal Devolution — It determines how that 41% share is distributed among individual states. It is determined by Income Distance (42.5%), Population (17.5%), Area (10%), Forest and Ecology (10%), Demographic Performance (10%)
& a 10% weight for contribution to GDP (added through 16th Finance Commission) eGrants- in-aid to states from the Consolidated Fund of India under Article 275.
Measures to improve finances of Panchayats and Municipalities.
